items.content:
Nov 11, 2026
ARTEX and VAPOR PANDA: How One Operator Used an Agentic AI Pentest Framework Against 200+ Organizations
Learn how VAPOR PANDA used the open-source ARTEX AI pentest framework to scale a China-nexus espionage campaign, and what defenders should detect, hunt for, and validate now.
Summary
What happened:
Over 11 days starting October 17, 2026, the China-nexus adversary CrowdStrike tracks as VAPOR PANDA used ARTEX, an open-source agentic AI pentest framework, to target more than 200 organizations in at least 14 countries from a single controller.
What’s new:
ARTEX didn’t introduce new exploits. It industrialized planning and memory, so one operator could run parallel attack paths and switch instantly when one failed.
How big the footprint is:
Censys found 1,465 internet-exposed ARTEX consoles (roughly 815 distinct deployments), and CrowdStrike, Microsoft, and India’s CERT-In have tied ARTEX to other threat actors, so attribution by tool no longer works.
What defenders should do:
Rotate exposed keys and credentials, enforce SAML signature validation and IMDSv2, run EDR everywhere, and alert on machine-speed activity like sub-lockout password sprays.
How SafeBreach helps:
SafeBreach’s new VAPOR PANDA ARTEX BLOODALCHEMY scenario that includes 10 steps and 22 attacks lets teams test whether their controls detect this AI-orchestrated attack chain.
Author:
adrian.culley@safebreach.com, Offensive Security Expert & Senior Sales Engineer
We’ve heard plenty of claims about
how AI is changing cyber attacks
. The ARTEX campaigns are the clearest evidence yet of what that change actually looks like, and it isn’t magic—it’s tempo.
On October 29, 2026,
CrowdStrike tied a campaign that began on October 17
to a China-nexus adversary it tracks as VAPOR PANDA. The operator ran the campaign through ARTEX, an open-source agentic AI pentest framework, and in 11 days reached more than 200 organizations in at least 14 countries from a single controller. The tradecraft underneath is familiar. What’s new is how many doors got tried at once.
A week later,
Censys counted 1,465 ARTEX consoles
exposed on the open internet, or roughly 815 distinct deployments once duplicates are stripped out. ARTEX is no longer one actor’s tool. It’s a free download that multiple threat actors are already using. Below, I’ll break down how ARTEX works, what VAPOR PANDA did with it, and what security teams should check, detect, and validate now.
PREFER TO LISTEN?
Adrian Culley joined host Tova Dvorin on episode 93 of The Cyber Resilience Brief: A SafeBreach Podcast to break down the ARTEX and VAPOR PANDA campaign.
Listen now
.
What is ARTEX?
ARTEX is an open-source agentic AI penetration testing framework
that uses a team of AI agents to plan and run attacks from reconnaissance through data exfiltration with little-to-no human interaction. A developer who goes by Autumn-27 published it on GitHub in July 2026, written in Go and pitched as a tool for authorized testing.
Here is how the architecture works:
Planner agents
choose the next move.
Worker agents
run the tools.
Results flow back
to the plan, and the plan adjusts.
Any model works:
ARTEX is model-agnostic, so any large language model (LLM) API will do.
Under the hood, published code analysis suggests ARTEX orchestrates familiar open-source tooling like Nuclei, sqlmap, Nmap, ffuf, and Playwright. The clever part is the bookkeeping: a shared graph of facts, findings, and goals; dead ends flagged after repeated retries; and parallel workers that each claim their own line of attack. That’s industrialized planning and memory, not a new exploit. The same analysis notes there’s no network-level scope enforcement. Scope lives in the prompt.
Does pulling the ARTEX repository make a difference?
Not much. The developer pulled the original repository in October, saying they weren’t involved in any attacks and the project was meant for authorized testing. By then,
Wiz
counted more than 12,000 forks. The code lives on in forks like ScopeWeaver and a commercial version called ARTEX PRO, and
TechCrunch
reports that dozens of copies are still on code-sharing sites.
Who is VAPOR PANDA?
VAPOR PANDA
is CrowdStrike’s name for a China-nexus espionage adversary that it first tracked as an activity cluster called VexatiousTemper, and that overlaps with what
Trend Micro calls Earth Estries
. CrowdStrike first saw the group in February 2021 exploiting the ProxyLogon chain against Microsoft Exchange (
CVE-2021-26855
and three related vulnerabilities).
Historically, VAPOR PANDA has targeted government, think tank, energy, and extractive organizations across Europe, North America, Oceania, and the UK to develop long-term access. The ARTEX campaign is its first observed use of AI tooling, which CrowdStrike judges is likely an expansion of scale rather than a change of mission. Pharma, semiconductors, nuclear, and defense are new sectors for the group.
How confident is the China-nexus attribution?
The attribution is CrowdStrike’s assessment: its intelligence team linked the ARTEX controller to VAPOR PANDA infrastructure. What’s visible publicly is circumstantial—operator instructions written in Chinese and labeled as human instruction, timestamps in China Standard Time, and a Chinese red-team nickname for the CrowdStrike Falcon sensor. CrowdStrike hedges the details with “likely.”
Why Attribution by Tool No Longer Works
ARTEX has already been tied to multiple, distinct threat actors, so knowing an attack used ARTEX tells you very little about who’s behind it. For example:
The South Korean financial campaign:
On October 7, 2026,
CrowdStrike reported
that an unattributed, Chinese-speaking, financially motivated operator (assessed with moderate confidence) used ARTEX against South Korean financial organizations.
Storm-0940:
On October 21, 2026,
Microsoft reported
that Storm-0940, a China state-aligned actor active since 2021, used ARTEX in a ConnectWise supply chain compromise followed by sign-in attempts at more than 2,250 Microsoft 365 tenants. CrowdStrike says Storm-0940 and VAPOR PANDA are distinct.
Crafty Falcon:
On November 4, 2026,
India’s Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) warned
financial and cryptocurrency organizations about a group it tracks as Crafty Falcon, which used ARTEX alongside PentAGI, Cairn, and CyberStrikeAI.
The Storm-0940 campaign shows both the speed and the limits of agentic attacks. Microsoft says the attackers moved fast enough that defenders had little time to detect and respond, with several cases reaching privileged access in under three hours. Yet most targeting failed: a separate October 10-14 password spray against 327 accounts at eight organizations, peaking at 2,900 failed sign-ins a minute, produced no successful authentication.
Two different China-nexus actors; one repository. For defenders, this means there is a need to detect the behavior, not the brand name, because the strings rotate, but the behavior doesn’t.
How did VAPOR PANDA use ARTEX?
VAPOR PANDA ran several engagements in parallel from one operator and one ARTEX controller. A main agent directed planner and worker agents, mostly running on DeepSeek. A human stepped in at decision points with instructions in Chinese. One instruction CrowdStrike translated told the agents to find hosts in the domain that weren’t running the Falcon sensor. That’s
MITRE ATT&CK
technique
T1518.001
(Security Software Discovery), used to find the unprotected hosts. Your coverage gaps are the attacker’s target list.
Pharmaceutical Intrusion #1: SAML, XXE, and Cloud Metadata
In one pharmaceutical intrusion, an unsigned Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) assertion accepted by the application was chained with an XML external entity (XXE) flaw to reach the cloud instance metadata service (
T1552.005
). That returned a role that could run commands on thousands of instances (
T1651
), and the agent then escalated to recover an enterprise administrator account. The unsigned assertion that opened the chain maps to forged SAML tokens (
T1606.002
). There was no zero-day anywhere in this chain—just a validation gap, a parser setting, and an exposed metadata endpoint. That’s why enforcing Instance Metadata Service Version 2 (IMDSv2) is on CrowdStrike’s list of recommendations.
Pharmaceutical Intrusion #2: Web Shells and Active Directory Abuse
The second pharmaceutical intrusion started with web shells (
T1505.003
), then an unauthenticated orchestration service that gave root in a production container environment. From there, the attackers read Local Administrator Password Solution (LAPS) passwords (
T1555
) and used resource-based constrained delegation (RBCD) to impersonate a privileged account (
T1134.001
).
This is textbook Active Directory abuse, chained by agents that switched to alternative approaches whenever a path failed. When one attack path fails, the agents switch to others instantly. We haven’t seen much of this in the past, and it makes defense much harder. If your testing stops because one attack path is closed, that won’t stop attackers using ARTEX. They’ll keep going.
The Greek Government Case: Old Credentials; New Economics
In a Greek government intrusion, a 2022 directory export from a mail server, with authentication keys that had likely not been rotated since the export, was used to forge an admin token and read mailboxes (
T1114.002
). A VPN configuration from a user’s sent mail, plus a VPN client key the operator described as coming from a May 2024 email leak, got the attackers into the internal network. These are years-old secrets, supplied by the operator and put to work by the agent because the cost of exploiting them has collapsed.
What is BLOODALCHEMY?
BLOODALCHEMY is the backdoor VAPOR PANDA deployed after gaining access, and CrowdStrike confirmed post-exploitation activity with it at nine organizations (it names the backdoor at a Middle East interior ministry and a Latin America foreign ministry). The backdoor was first
publicly documented in October 2023
. The loader is classic DLL side-loading (
T1574.001
): a GameHook binary renamed svchost.exe (
T1036.005
), a malicious DLL called graphics-hook-filter64.dll beside it, and an encrypted payload, all staged in exposed open directories. The AI isn’t writing novel malware. An established toolkit is being delivered at agent speed.
Initial Access and Infrastructure
Beyond the SAML flaw, CrowdStrike saw a mix of initial access techniques: exploitation of public-facing applications (
T1190
), external remote services (
T1133
), valid accounts (
T1078
), and password spraying (
T1110.003
) against at least 12 more organizations, including US think tanks and European government bodies. To maintain access and hide their traffic, the attackers also used web shells, Chisel and SoftEther tunnels, and Tor and SOCKS proxies (
T1090.003
and
T1572
). To be clear, the 12 additional organizations were sprayed, but not necessarily breached.
How many organizations did VAPOR PANDA compromise?
The 200-plus figure counts organizations targeted, not organizations compromised, so it’s worth handling with care. The targets spanned at least 14 countries and included:
Foreign ministries in Latin America, Europe, Asia, and the Middle East
19 US organizations across pharma, semiconductors, defense, nuclear, and finance
Telecommunications companies in the US, Belgium, and the Philippines
CrowdStrike confirmed post-exploitation activity at nine organizations, with password spraying against at least 12 more. Some coverage, including
CyberScoop’s
, cites a larger figure of roughly 140 targets that CrowdStrike assessed as confirmed or moderate-confidence compromises. Either way, these categories don’t add up to a clean success rate. It’s a wide net with a smaller confirmed core.
What about the South Korean campaign?
We shouldn’t lose sight of the person behind the agents. In the South Korean case, the operator ran ARTEX with DeepSeek as the primary model and Claude Code sessions alongside it, including sessions backed by GLM-5.3 and Grok 4.6. We know those details only because the operator’s own servers were exposed, holding Claude Code session histories, ARTEX configurations, and Claude memory files. CrowdStrike names no banks and gives no victim counts, and press accounts differ:
Infosecurity Magazine
reports 25,000 and 40,000 people affected at two institutions, while
BleepingComputer
names three large banks. Treat those details as unsettled.
How many ARTEX consoles are exposed online?
Censys
counted 1,465 hosts worldwide exposing an ARTEX console to the public internet. About 650 of those sit in two blocks of identically configured hosting, which leaves roughly 815 distinct-looking deployments—the source of TechCrunch’s figure of more than 800. Not every deployment is hostile, and many will belong to authorized testers, but it’s a far bigger footprint than a handful of named campaigns.
Censys also found other threat tooling on 155 of those hosts (10.6%):
Common post-exploitation frameworks:
Cobalt Strike, Vshell, and Adaptix C2
Other AI attack frameworks:
CyberStrikeAI appears alongside ARTEX on 70 hosts
Open directories:
32 hosts expose directories of attack tools, post-exploitation kits, stagers, and implants
Self-hosted LLM gateways:
43 hosts run LLM gateway software, so model access, often through reseller proxies, is part of the operators’ stack
The takeaway from Censys is that operators appear to be running multiple agent frameworks side by side.
ARTEX doesn’t need to be exposed to the internet to work. According to
TechCrunch
, Censys researcher Silas Cutler says the software doesn’t require internet exposure, so this reads as misconfiguration. TechCrunch describes the consoles as open without a password, while other write-ups say only that they’re exposed, so how many are truly unauthenticated is still an open question. TechCrunch also reports that one instance tied to a Korean campaign was exposed for months (Censys’s own post dates that open directory to August 18, about seven weeks before the CrowdStrike’s report), with attack data reaching payment and gaming companies beyond the banks.
Is ARTEX a super weapon?
No. A separate
Check Point analysis
found that agentic frameworks like ARTEX can run large-scale attacks with little human input for a few hundred dollars, but they still sometimes fail and sometimes hallucinate their own success. They’re cheap and noisy. That’s bad news for volume, but decent news for detection, because noisy, machine-paced activity is something a security operations center (SOC) can detect and alert on based on a pattern.
The exposed controllers are both good news and bad news. They hand researchers playbooks, targets, and implants. But the risk is that your organization’s name sits in someone else’s exposed attack data, and you hear about it from a researcher first. And if your own red team runs agentic tooling, make sure its controller isn’t reachable from the internet.
TechCrunch also notes that many ARTEX-linked attacks exploited weak or known passwords and missing multi-factor authentication (MFA), which matches everything in this campaign. The agents aren’t beating strong controls. They’re walking through the unglamorous gaps in basic cyber hygiene, at scale.
How should security teams respond to ARTEX?
Start with the basics CrowdStrike recommends, then tune detections for machine-speed activity.
What does CrowdStrike recommend?
Rotate keys and credentials after any suspected exposure.
Enforce SAML signature validation and IMDSv2.
Patch internet-facing appliances.
Run endpoint detection and response (EDR) everywhere.
Hunt for ARTEX markers: command lines containing “artx” or “artex,” cloud roles with an “artx” prefix, comments starting with “art18-,” and a folder called artx5v under C:\ProgramData. Treat these as leads, not proof. Anyone can fork the repo and change a string.
What should SOC teams look for in the logs?
At the speed these agents work, cadence is the signal. Look for:
Password sprays against Microsoft Entra ID and Okta, a second apart
Rapid-fire cloud enumeration (one write-up cites 27 events in 23 seconds)
Vendor app sign-ins from unfamiliar IP addresses
New credentials added to service principals
Sudden privileged role assignments
Your existing spray and access-denied detections already apply. Most teams just aren’t alerting on that cadence.
How can you test your defenses against VAPOR PANDA and ARTEX?
Once you’ve checked those controls, you still need to know whether they work together against the real attack chain. That’s where
adversarial exposure validation
comes in. SafeBreach has released a VAPOR PANDA ARTEX BLOODALCHEMY scenario in the SafeBreach platform—10 steps and 22 attacks that follow the campaign:
Password spraying kept below the lockout threshold
Credential theft from the AWS, Azure, and GCP metadata services
Remote command execution through Azure VM Run Command
Side-loaded loader execution and persistence
Web shell traffic
DCSync
Security software discovery
Command and control and exfiltration over Tor
The scenario doesn’t include the BLOODALCHEMY samples themselves, SoftEther and Chisel tunneling, the unsigned SAML plus XXE web attack, RBCD abuse, or remote mailbox collection. SafeBreach’s attack path propagation capabilities add the LAPS password read over LDAP and installed EDR enumeration—the same step the operator used to hunt for unprotected hosts. The cloud steps require cloud simulators, and the Active Directory steps require a domain-joined simulator.
The real question isn’t, “Do we have a signature for BLOODALCHEMY?” It’s whether a sub-threshold password spray, a metadata call from a cloud instance, and a renamed binary side-loading a DLL get noticed in your environment today.
What to Watch Next
I’m watching four things as this develops:
More Censys findings:
whether Censys and others publish more on what those exposed controllers held
New attributions:
whether another China-nexus group is publicly tied to ARTEX
Fork evolution:
whether the forks diverge into something more capable than the original
Operator mistakes:
whether operators keep making the South Korean-style operational security mistakes that let us see the playbook
It also echoes a question we raised in our
analysis of the SecFlow AI intrusion harness
: whether AI harnesses verify their own claims. CrowdStrike expects China-nexus adversaries to keep adopting agentic frameworks like ARTEX over the next 12 months.
The Bottom Line
ARTEX didn’t invent new attacks. It made old ones cheap, fast, and parallel. Check your credentials, check your coverage, and test whether you can catch the attack as it unfolds. And if you’re running these tools yourself, secure the controller.

No. CrowdStrike says Storm-0940 and VAPOR PANDA are distinct, even though both are China-aligned and both used ARTEX. Microsoft attributes Storm-0940 to a ConnectWise supply chain compromise followed by sign-in attempts at more than 2,250 Microsoft 365 tenants. Because ARTEX is freely available, the tool alone can’t tell you which actor is behind an attack.
How many ARTEX consoles are exposed on the internet?
Censys researchers counted 1,465 hosts exposing an ARTEX console to the public internet as of early November 2026. About 650 of those sit in two blocks of identically configured hosting, leaving roughly 815 distinct deployments. Censys also found other threat tooling, including Cobalt Strike, Vshell, and CyberStrikeAI on 155 of those hosts.
How can SOC teams detect ARTEX-driven attacks?
SOC teams can detect ARTEX-driven attacks by alerting on machine-speed cadence rather than specific strings. Warning signs include password sprays against Microsoft Entra ID or Okta a second apart, rapid-fire cloud enumeration, vendor app sign-ins from unfamiliar IP addresses, new credentials on service principals, and sudden privileged role assignments. Strings like “artx” in command lines are useful leads, but forks can change them.
Does AI make attacks like VAPOR PANDA’s unstoppable?
No. In the VAPOR PANDA campaign, the AI agents didn’t use zero-days or novel malware. They exploited unrotated keys, weak passwords, missing multi-factor authentication (MFA), and misconfigurations at scale. Check Point’s analysis also found that agentic frameworks like ARTEX sometimes fail and hallucinate their own success, which makes their noisy, machine-paced activity detectable.
How does SafeBreach help organizations defend against ARTEX attacks?

ARTEX AI Attack Framework: SafeBreach Coverage for FBI FLASH Alert FLASH-20261113-001
Learn how SafeBreach maps FBI FLASH-20261113-001 to simulations that test your exposure to the ARTEX AI attack framework’s machine-speed cloud, identity, and Active Directory intrusions.
Summary
One framework, many operators:
FBI FLASH Alert FLASH-20261113-001 (November 13, 2026) warns that a variety of malicious cyber actors have used ARTEX, an open-source AI penetration testing framework, since at least August 2026.
Machine-speed intrusions:
ARTEX turns a plain-language goal into commands run by multiple AI agents, and the FBI cites Microsoft reporting that some ARTEX intrusions reached privileged access in under three hours.
Old weaknesses, no zero-days:
FLASH-20261113-001 cites no CVEs. ARTEX operators exploit known flaws such as unsigned SAML assertions, hardcoded passwords, and unrotated keys across overlooked cloud, identity, and Active Directory surfaces.
Two named campaigns:
The FBI links ARTEX to data theft affecting approximately 67,000 people at South Korean financial institutions and a ConnectWise Cloud Backup supply chain compromise reaching more than 2,250 downstream Microsoft 365 tenants.
SafeBreach coverage:
SafeBreach customers already have coverage against the majority of the ARTEX TTPs in FLASH-20261113-001, from Azure and AWS metadata credential theft to Kerberoasting, Pass-the-Ticket, and Tor-based C2, and the SafeBreach research team is adding new simulations mapped to the FLASH.
Author:
Tova Dvorin, Senior Product Marketing Manager
On November 13, 2026, the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) released
FLASH Alert FLASH-20261113-001: “Threat Overview of ARTEX Autonomous Penetration Testing Framework”
. The FLASH provides intelligence on how malicious cyber actors use the ARTEX framework, including tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) mapped to MITRE ATT&CK, indicators of compromise (IOCs), and recommended mitigations.
The FLASH focuses on a tool rather than a single threat group. According to the FBI, ARTEX lets actors with limited technical expertise run multi-target intrusions at machine speed, often against peripheral, less-protected systems.
For more information, read the full FBI FLASH
here
.
What Is ARTEX and Which Threat Actors Use It?
ARTEX is an open-source, multi-agent penetration testing platform written in Go. It turns a natural-language objective into machine commands executed by what the FBI calls “super intelligence (SI) agents”—AI agents driven by large language models (LLMs)—with minimal human involvement beyond setting the goal.
ARTEX has no model of its own. It connects to external LLM providers, including Anthropic Claude, OpenAI GPT, DeepSeek, GLM, Grok, and Kimi, and the FBI reports that attacker-controlled instances most often run Chinese-developed models led by the DeepSeek Flash family. Guardrails at any single AI provider are not a control defenders can rely on.
A developer using the handle “Autumn-27” released ARTEX on GitHub in July 2026 and made the repository unavailable on October 8, 2026, after reports of abuse. ARTEX still circulates through community forks, localized variations, archived copies, and a commercial version, ARTEX PRO. Censys counted over 1,600 publicly exposed ARTEX consoles in early November 2026, a number the FBI says is likely significantly higher.
The FBI names no state sponsor. It describes a variety of actors targeting ten sectors: financial services, government, technology, defense, semiconductor, energy, healthcare, manufacturing, telecommunications, and legal.
Two campaigns stand out:
South Korean financial institutions:
a financially motivated campaign that exfiltrated personal information on approximately 67,000 individuals.
ConnectWise Cloud Backup:
a supply chain compromise in which actors abused a trusted ConnectWise application to reach more than 2,250 downstream Microsoft 365 tenants.
The FLASH’s indicator tables also tie ARTEX infrastructure to Microsoft-tracked Storm-3358, active as recently as November 6, 2026. SafeBreach Threat Research assesses that Storm-3358 and VAPOR PANDA, the China-nexus actor tracked by CrowdStrike, lead the observed campaigns. For VAPOR PANDA’s campaign in depth, see our earlier analysis,
ARTEX and VAPOR PANDA: How One Operator Used an Agentic AI Pentest Framework Against 200+ Organizations
. Other recent FBI FLASH alerts we have covered include
TeamPCP Supply Chain Attacks (FLASH-20260702-01)
.
ARTEX TTPs Mapped to MITRE ATT&CK
ARTEX introduces no new exploits. Its AI agents chain familiar techniques in parallel and at machine speed. The FLASH groups observed activity by intrusion phase; the sections below follow those phases and the MITRE ATT&CK techniques the FBI cites.
Reconnaissance and Discovery: Sub-Second Cloud Permission Mapping
ARTEX agents map the effective permissions of Azure credentials, shared access signature (SAS) tokens, service principals, and storage account keys with sub-second capability checks, then test blob writes and deletes. Through Microsoft Graph, they enumerate users, mailboxes, and applications. In AWS, they use DryRun flags to test what a compromised Identity and Access Management (IAM) user can do.

The FBI lists familiar entry points: unsigned SAML assertions, XML external entity (XXE) injection, server-side request forgery (SSRF), SQL and command injection, hardcoded administrator passwords in JavaScript bundles, missing API authentication, weak admin credentials, and stolen VPN configurations. ARTEX operators also abuse cross-account cloud trust and vendor credentials to pivot through B2B federation from a weaker supplier into a higher-value network. In the ConnectWise campaign, actors hijacked a trusted OAuth application to reach downstream Microsoft 365 tenants.

ARTEX agents establish footholds with JSP and PHP web shells, including one planted through MySQL log poisoning; SafeBreach Threat Research identified the R57 and WSO PHP web shells among them. In the cloud, they abuse Kudu administrative APIs, create new administrator accounts, add secrets to service principals and existing OAuth applications, create SSH key pairs, and allocate Elastic IPs. The FLASH also lists the open-source remote access tools WISP, vshell, and AdaptixC2, along with the BLOODALCHEMY backdoor, which a signed GameHook executable renamed to svchost.exe loads by side-loading a malicious DLL.

Privilege Escalation: Kerberoasting, DCSync, and Forged Admin Tokens
ARTEX agents launch cloud instances with high-value IAM roles, use XXE to reach the cloud metadata service, and forge administrator tokens from unrotated authentication keys. In Active Directory, the FLASH describes Kerberoasting, DCSync to steal the domain krbtgt key, and resource-based constrained delegation abuse.

Discovery: AD Enumeration, LAPS Reads, and EDR Coverage Gaps
Inside the network, ARTEX agents run iterative PowerShell enumeration against domain controllers, enumerate more than 110,000 Active Directory objects, and read Local Administrator Password Solution (LAPS) passwords. They also inventory endpoint sensor coverage to find Windows machines without a specific endpoint detection and response (EDR) product—the hosts least likely to raise an alert.

Lateral Movement: Pass-the-Ticket, WinRM, and Kerberos Relay
ARTEX agents attempt Pass-the-Ticket, Windows Remote Management (WinRM), Kerberos relay, and Pass-the-Hash toward domain controllers. SafeBreach Threat Research ties these chains to Mimikatz, which harvests plaintext credentials, NTLM hashes, and Kerberos tickets from LSASS. The FLASH notes that endpoint protection blocked the Pass-the-Hash attempts: where a sensor was present and working, it did its job.

Collection: Mass Data Reads and Staging for Exfiltration
ARTEX agents interrogate backend SQL databases, perform mass blob reads, run custom EC2 boot scripts to harvest data, read mailboxes on compromised mail servers, and create 100 GB volumes to stage data. Command output goes to rotating webhook.site endpoints.

Command and Control: Residential Proxies, Tor, and Tunneling
ARTEX operators route command and control (C2) through residential proxies, Tor, SOCKS proxies, and compromised relays, tunnel traffic with Chisel and SoftEther, and use C2 domains associated with the BLOODALCHEMY backdoor.

FBI FLASH-20261113-001 provides network and behavioral IOCs rather than file hashes, including:

tied to ARTEX servers, South Korean campaign proxies, the ConnectWise campaign, and Storm-3358 C2 nodes

to hunt for: BLOODALCHEMY, WISP, vshell, AdaptixC2, and the LLM proxy software CLIProxyAPI and New API
Behavioral indicators
, such as LLM API calls from systems with no business need, high-frequency sequential requests against login and search endpoints, and .aspx or .jsp files in unexpected web paths
The FBI cautions that cloud-hosted IP addresses are frequently reassigned, so vet each indicator against your own telemetry before blocking. For the full indicator set, refer to the
FBI FLASH

Cloud and Identity Mitigations Recommended in FLASH-20261113-001
Inventory every internet-facing application
, including partner portals, mobile backends, legacy services, third-party integrations, and apps built by individual business units.
Take the management plane off the internet
by restricting cloud administration, Kudu/SCM, hypervisor, and backup interfaces to trusted networks.
Apply least privilege to multi-tenant app permissions and consent grants

Scan repositories, pipelines, and container images for embedded secrets

should review every affected Microsoft 365 tenant by application ID from at least October 1, 2026, and preserve evidence before removing credentials or grants.

Sub-second cloud probing:
rapid blob write-and-delete tests, ARM dry-run validations, AWS DryRun checks, PassRole operations, and metadata service queries.
LLM egress:
calls to LLM APIs or proxy software such as CLIProxyAPI and New API from systems with no business need, and unexplained AI token or billing spikes.
Agentic noise:
compressed bursts of activity, high volumes of failed attempts with small iterative changes, and duplicate requests from overlapping sub-agents.
Identity changes:
service principal sign-ins from unusual ASNs or hosting providers, new OAuth credentials, SSH key additions, and unexpected VM launches.
Footholds:
web shells in unexpected paths and WISP, vshell, AdaptixC2, or BLOODALCHEMY components.

会检查模型在内部工作负载和受支持的外部部署中的推理与行动。它可以自动标记未经授权的行为，并在支持的情况下暂停工作负载或对话。
对齐
两款模型在大多数对齐评估中的表现与 GPT-6 Astra 相近，并在模拟职场任务中采取了更少的不当行动。不过，在两项测试中，它们更容易漏报阻碍工作的问题，例如文件缺失或搜索工具不可用。我们在 Codex 中添加了指令，大幅减少了此类遗漏，并将继续研究这一行为。
在“隐瞒任务障碍”评估中，我们在编程任务中设置障碍，例如移除用户要求智能体编辑的文件。评估考察模型是否会向用户说明这一障碍。
定价与可用性
即日起，所有 Plus、Pro、Enterprise 和 Edu 用户都可在 ChatGPT 工作和 Codex 中使用 GPT-6.2 Astra 和 Sol。Pro 500 订阅用户可为这两款模型启用超高速模式。我们还首次向 Pro 200 订阅用户开放超高速模式，率先支持 GPT-6.2 Sol。符合条件的 Enterprise 和 Edu 用户，在工作空间管理员启用后，也可获得相同访问权限。开发者也可通过 OpenAI API 使用
gpt-6.2-astra
和
gpt-6.2-sol
，两款模型在发布时均支持超高速模式。
得益于更高的 Token 使用效率、输入和输出 Token 价格降低 20%，以及缓存输入 Token 价格进一步降低 60%，GPT‑6.2 Astra 的单项任务成本显著低于 GPT‑6 Astra。标准 API 定价按每百万 Token 计：输入 8 美元，缓存输入 0.40 美元，输出 40 美元。GPT‑6.2 Sol 沿用 GPT‑6.1 Sol 的定价，每百万 Token 的输入价格为 2 美元，缓存输入为 0.10 美元，输出为 10 美元。
使用 GPT-6.2 Astra 和 Sol 时，为提高缓存复用率、帮助降低成本和延迟，并跨轮次保留推理，我们建议
保持提示词前缀不变，并在对话中追加新指令⁠
（在新窗口中打开）
。
2026 年
作者
OpenAI

Artificial Analysis⁠

的报告，使用 mini-swe-agent 执行框架。Anthropic 报告称，Fable 5.2 在 Claude Code 中以 Max 推理强度取得了 74.6% 的得分。

items.target: 路演喊三天平替英伟达，PPT 小字却写着仅限预填充：看清 AI 自动写算子的真边界
items.text: yage-share published: 路演喊三天平替英伟达，PPT 小字却写着仅限预填充：看清 AI 自动写算子的真边界
items.title: 路演喊三天平替英伟达，PPT 小字却写着仅限预填充：看清 AI 自动写算子的真边界
items.content:
今年 11 月 10 日，Anthropic 正式启动 IPO
路演，并在官网放出了一段公开路演视频。在这段视频中，联合创始人兼首席算力官
Tom Brown
提到，以往引入一款新芯片通常需要几十位工程师花好几个月，但这次他们使用内部模型
Mythos，基本没有人工干预，仅用 3 天就让 Claude 在 AMD
显卡上跑了起来，独立编写了将近 100% 的底层算子。
底层算子是在显卡硬件上直接运行的底层计算小程序，负责矩阵乘法等基础运算。这段视频传开后，社交媒体上出现了许多超过
50 万阅读的帖子，宣称英伟达的 CUDA
护城河已经消失。然而，翻看这段路演视频的完整字幕就会发现，其中从未提及英伟达和
CUDA。
如果暂停视频，看左下角的灰色小字，或者翻一下同一天交给美国证监会的
法定招股书修正案
，就会发现完全不同的剧本。在这份监管文件里，3
天和底层算子这两个词一次都没出现。但同一天公布的私募名单显示，英伟达和谷歌并列第一，分别出资
100
亿美元购买公司股票。为什么路演高调造势，法定文件只字不提，英伟达还砸钱认购？答案就在
PPT 左下角两行小字里。
路演 PPT
左下角那两行灰字，悄悄划掉了哪三件事
回到
路演视频转写实录
对应的画面里，左边那条橙色曲线标注着使用
Mythos 约 3 天到顶点，右边绿色曲线标注着传统方法需要 6 到 12
个月。但左下角的灰色小字加了三个限定：只针对单一模型，只在单台 AMD
MI355X 多卡服务器上运行，并且只把提示词处理拉到可用性能水平。
其中最关键的限制是只实现了预填充阶段。正如
我们之前讲大模型预填充与解码分离的文章
所介绍的，大模型处理一次对话分为截然不同的两步。第一步叫预填充阶段，也就是
PPT
小字里的提示词处理，相当于模型一次性读题，把用户塞进来的整段文字拼成一个大矩阵一口气算完，主要吃单张显卡的计算力。第二步叫解码阶段，相当于模型一个字一个字往外写回答，每蹦出一个字都要把几百
GB
的模型参数和历史缓存从显存里重新搬运一遍，主要卡在显存带宽和跨卡通信上。
AI 为什么能 3
天写出预填充阶段的底层算子？因为单机预填充就是个封闭练习场，在一台机器上做读题计算，每个底层算子就几百行代码，输入输出规整。工程师把英伟达显卡算出来的结果当标准答案，让模型昼夜改代码跑测试，编译器几秒就能判分。这种目标明确、几秒自动反馈的封闭循环，正是编程智能体最擅长的舒适区。反观右边那条
6 到 12
个月的传统曲线，涵盖的是把预填充阶段、解码阶段和模型训练全套搬上生产线的完整工期。拿单机读题热身的
3
天，直接去比全栈投产的大半年，本身就是拿热身赛成绩去比全运会总工期。
单机预填充封闭靶场与全栈生产上线的工程边界对比
走出单机预填充，多芯片上线真正要命的坑长什么样
既然预填充阶段的底层算子几天就能跑通，剩下那大半年，人类工程师到底在跟什么死磕？一旦从单机读题迈向跨几十张卡的解码阶段和大规模训练，难题就变了性质。大模型单张显卡装不下，必须拆成碎片放在几十张芯片上同时算。每生成一个新字，几十张芯片都要一边高速同步数据，一边在小数点后几位上对齐概率、挑出最高分的词。
Anthropic 在今年 9 月发布的
近期三起线上故障复盘报告
，展示了深水区的真实面貌。当时许多开发者抱怨
Claude
突然变笨甚至胡言乱语。团队追查数周发现，问题没有一个出在单机预填充阶段的底层算子上，全都出在多芯片解码阶段采样和底层编译器等环节。其中有两起故障直接发生在这套多芯片集群的
Google TPU 服务器上。
第一个故障来自 Google TPU
服务器的解码阶段。工程团队做了一项运行时优化，但模型在生成英文代码时，偶尔会给一些生僻字分配高概率。用户在用英文写代码，中间突然出现一个泰语问候语或者中文字符，花了整整
8 天才回滚修复。
第二个故障更隐蔽，潜伏了整整 8 个月。TPU
集群的解码阶段，几十张芯片各自用 16 位浮点数算词元概率后要汇总排序，但
TPU 底层编译器默认开启了超额精度优化，自动把一部分运算升成 32
位浮点数。不同芯片的小数点精度对不上，在汇总谁是第一名时产生分歧，直接把最该输出的词弄丢了。
工程师重写采样代码去修这个精度漏洞，结果又踩到了底层快速近似排序算法里的另一个编译器暗坑。这个暗坑在普通处理器上完全正常，在
TPU
上也只有撞上特定请求批次大小才会算错。只要一打开调试工具或改动计算步骤顺序，故障就会自动消失。团队最终只能放弃快速近似排序算法，退回精确排序。要把这类特定批次下才发作、打开调试器就消失的跨芯片暗坑一个个揪出来填平，靠单机跑几天代码生成无济于事。
招股书删掉三天宣传之后，真正替
AI 兜底的考场是谁造的
回到那份受证券法规严格约束的招股书修正案。Anthropic
删掉了短期移植宣传，在第 137 页和第 208
页写下了实情：团队能加快新芯片上线，靠的是耗时数年、投入巨资在多芯片家族上建立的扎实基础，核心是一套专有测试编排层。
专有测试编排层是一个能够模拟真实业务负载、在不同芯片家族之间进行自动化测试和性能比较的内部基础设施。Mythos
之所以能在短时间内写出实用的底层算子，是因为人类工程师花了数年时间构建了一套可以回放真实线上流量、自动对比精度、随时拦截异常的自动化测试考场。
举个例子，在路演的前一天，一个开源组织OpenRSI和开源多模态推理框架团队发布了关于
SGLang-Omni自动调优的实测报告
。报告里可以看到，智能体自己提出假设、改代码，在4到7个小时内找到了第一批加速方案，比如把空转等待的线程休眠一下就提升了32.5%的实时输出吞吐量。
但报告作者特别指出，评估器才是真正的产品。如果只让智能体追求速度，它会为了刷分悄悄降低回答质量。因此，任务定义、边算边播的系统架构设计、把智能体隔绝在外的防作弊验证程序全由人类工程师手写完成。即便智能体交卷时附带了实测数据，人类维护者审查并合入每个补丁，中位数花了
3.5 天，单个补丁最多来回修改了 23
次提交。所谓零人工写代码，其实是人类把精力从亲手写底层算子，转移到了建造专有测试编排层和事后把关上。
路演口播、PPT
小字与招股书真话的三层落差及验证沙盒分工
手握四倍算力倍增器，为什么还要签
9000 亿美元买卡合同
招股书显示，Anthropic 签下的长期算力采购承诺总额已接近 9000
亿美元。面对这笔巨额账单，路演视频用一道乘法来概括算力效率：总有效算力 =
物理芯片容量 ×
算力倍增器。算力倍增器指通过改进算法或底层软件，让同样数量的物理芯片跑出数倍有效算力的技术手段。首席财务官也在视频里展示了成绩单：过去
6 个季度里，公司单位美元算力换回的营业收入翻了 4.3 倍。
然而细看招股书的季度明细表，会发现这个指标在今年二季度冲到 2.08
美元的高点后，到了三季度反而掉头向下。原因就写在招股书里：长期合同的芯片交付跟不上需求，公司在三季度不得不掏出
50
亿美元买高价现货算力。算力倍增器再精妙，也变不出显卡和电力，一旦芯片交付断档，照样得去现货市场高价补缺口。
更关键的是，Tom Brown 在路演中坦率地承认了这一点。公司拥有 4
倍的算力倍增器后，虽然能省下 75%
的算力成本训练出相同的模型，但前沿实验室的目标永远是投入全部物理算力，去训练过去想象不到的更大模型。软件效率越高，对买卡的需求反而越迫切。
那省不出买卡的钱，同时支持英伟达、AMD、谷歌和亚马逊这 4 家芯片、让 AI
能快速移植预填充阶段的底层算子有什么商业价值呢？答案藏在这家公司当天公布的合同变动里。Anthropic
在 8 月刚刚签下了算力供应商 Lambda 的 349 亿美元大单，但因为 Lambda
没能按时拿到机房租约，所以这份合同现在可以随时解约。在同一天，公司对微软英伟达集群的最低采购额也提高到了
472 亿美元。
看懂这笔账，整场路演的算力故事就顺理成章了。AI
自动写底层算子和多芯片策略，目标从来不是消灭英伟达，也不会缩减买卡规模。一旦某家算力商机房掉链子，或者某款芯片漫天要价，团队随时能把预填充阶段等大吞吐任务切到别家芯片上跑。在总额近
9000 亿美元的算力牌桌上，3
天跑通预填充阶段并非掀翻牌桌的锤子，而是让卖卡巨头都不敢轻易断供或坐地起价的换轨底牌。

items.text: yage-share published: 给 Agent 接 DeepSeek 新出的全家桶 API，真正好用的是那几个独立接口
items.title: 给 Agent 接 DeepSeek 新出的全家桶 API，真正好用的是那几个独立接口
items.content:
以前，很多人都认为 DeepSeek 的官方网页版和手机端比开发者的 API
更实用。这是因为官方客户端提供了联网搜索、阅读网页链接、解析几十页长的文档以及语音朗读等周边功能，而开发者的
API 只能进行纯文本对话。2026 年 11 月 13 日，DeepSeek 发布了
全套应用接口公告
，将这些官方客户端中的周边功能作为
API 一次全部开放，并开源了一个可以立即使用的网页前端项目
chat-demo
。
这次开放的接口提供了两种截然不同的调用方式：一种是内置全家桶开关，调用轻量模型
deepseek-flash
聊天时直接在请求里打开联网搜索或读文档的开关，DeepSeek
服务端就会自动在后台搜网页、读链接，最后把整理好的现成回答返回给你；另一种是独立工具接口，DeepSeek
把底层的网页搜索、网页抓取、文档识别、语音识别和语音合成单独拆成了 5
个接口，就算不调用 DeepSeek
的大模型，也能把这些接口单独拿来当搜索引擎、网页转 Markdown
爬虫或文档识别器用。很多开发者的第一反应是去用省事的第一种内置全家桶开关。但只要翻开
DeepSeek
的技术文档、动手往自己的智能体代码里接一次就会发现，这套内置开关是个连自定义工具都不允许混用的封闭黑盒，常规的智能体接不进去。真正给所有开发者带来实惠的，是
DeepSeek 单独拆出来低价售卖的独立工具接口。
为什么省事的对话内置开关，反而接不进常规的
Agent？
开发者看到第一种内置全家桶开关只需在对话请求里加个参数就能自动联网和读文档，第一反应就是把现有的智能体代码加上这个开关，少写几行工具调用的胶水代码。而且早些时候
OpenAI 的 Responses API 和 Anthropic 的 Messages API
也都推出了类似的服务器端内置搜索工具，为什么海外大厂的内置工具可以接进智能体，DeepSeek
的内置全家桶开关反而接不进去呢？
这背后的原因是，OpenAI 对 Responses API
的定位是提供一个通用的云端运行平台，它可以在这个平台上保存对话历史状态，并且把官方内置的搜索工具和代码沙盒跟开发者自己的业务函数（下称自定义工具）混在一起调用。但
DeepSeek 虽然兼容了 Responses API
的请求格式，却没有提供一个通用的云端运行平台。DeepSeek 的 API
文档明确说它不支持保存会话历史状态，也直接忽略了代码沙盒、向量检索等传入参数。研发人员走了一条更省事的捷径：把自家官方网页版内部用强化学习训练好的固定后端流水线直接暴露出来，而且仅支持轻量模型
deepseek-flash
。这样直接暴露内部流水线的设计，就带来了三个直接限制。
第一个限制是开启内置开关后禁止混用自定义工具。平时做智能体应用，往往需要用到各种自定义工具，比如查询内部数据库、读写本地文件等等。但是，DeepSeek
的
搭建对话机器人的指南
里面明确提到，如果你开启了内置的联网搜索、读取网页链接、高水位安全审核、会话标题生成中任何一个功能，那么这个请求就不能同时指定任何自定义工具，否则就会返回一个
400
错误码。这就让内置的全家桶开关没办法接入任何需要执行外部动作的业务系统。
第二个限制是锁死模型参数与输出格式。开启这些开关后，请求中指定的采样温度、核采样率、停止词和思考预算等控制参数全部静默失效。如果业务代码依赖模型返回
JSON
结构化格式，或者需要助手消息前缀续写，开启联网或安全审核开关后同样会直接报错。就连给模型传入当天日期和所在城市的方式，也必须严格照搬
DeepSeek
官方网页版的内部协议。平时写应用，开发者习惯把当天日期写进顶层的系统提示词里；但如果每天日期一变就改系统提示词，此前攒下的历史对话前缀缓存就会全部失效。为了保住前缀缓存命中率，DeepSeek
要求开发者必须在每条用户消息之前，紧挨着塞入一条固定格式的
latest_reminder
角色消息来传递日期和地点，放错位置同样会报错。
第三个限制是网页正文加密与上下文清理。为了防止外部开发者把内置工具当成免费爬虫，内置搜索和深度思考搜索返回的结果块里，网页内容全部加密成了密文，客户端拿不到明文。到了下一轮对话，这些搜索结果还会从模型的上下文记忆里清除，只留下上一轮的回答文本。内置读链接工具返回的网页正文字段干脆恒为空字符串，加密后的内容藏在签名字段里，多轮对话时必须由客户端把整块签名原样传回服务端做内部拼接。这套防线决定了内置全家桶开关只适合配合官方开源的
chat-demo
前端，原样克隆一个纯聊天网站。
不绑大模型的独立工具接口，是怎么把搜索和解析价格压下来的？
既然内置全家桶开关是个封闭黑盒，普通智能体开发者能从这次更新里拿到什么实惠？答案藏在公告后半截。正因为内置全家桶开关无法与自定义工具共存，连
OpenAI 官方的编程助手 Codex
接进来都用不了那套内置搜索。为了解决这个冲突，DeepSeek
在同一天把底层的网页搜索、网页抓取、文档识别、语音识别和语音合成，全部做成了不绑定大模型对话、可以单独调用的独立工具接口。在官方同步更新的
Codex
一键配置脚本里，研发团队就是直接为模型默认开启了独立联网搜索通道，让
Codex 绕开内置模式，直接调用底层的搜索与抓取接口。
这种把底层工具拆出来单卖的做法，走到了海外大厂的反面。在 OpenAI 和
Anthropic 的体系里，联网搜索固定焊死在大模型推理流程中。你不调用 GPT 或
Claude，就没法单独使用它们的搜索能力，而且每搜索 1000 次要交 10
美元的工具调用费，检索内容拼入上下文后还要另付模型词元费。DeepSeek
的独立工具接口则不需要调用它的大模型。哪怕你的智能体用 GPT 或 Claude
当主脑，也能直接拿 DeepSeek
的密钥去调它的搜索和抓取接口。对比下方的价格就能看出，它的搜索与网页抓取每千次仅收
5 元人民币，搜索失败或结果为空还不扣费，单价不到海外大厂的十分之一。
而更省钱的一点是，DeepSeek 的自建搜索引擎有一个全文返回的特性。在
网页搜索与抓取指南
中，DeepSeek
首次披露了其独立搜索接口是由 DeepSeek
自己研发的搜索引擎提供支持。这个引擎针对智能体做了优化，在进行搜索时不仅可以提供关键词，还可以额外提供用户的原始提问来帮助引擎理解意图。每个搜索结果不仅有相关性分数、网站权威度和简短摘要，还有一个围绕原始提问提取的
800 字左右高密度摘要。此外，如果在搜索请求中包含
need_content
参数，还会返回每个搜索结果的 Markdown
格式完整正文。不论单条查询返回默认数量还是最多 50
篇结果，开启全文返回都不会增加单次搜索的价格，仍然只收半毛钱人民币。相比之下，第三方的搜索工具
Firecrawl
则会根据返回的网页数量逐页收取积分，搜一次再抓十几个网页的全文，成本要高出十倍以上。
除此之外，独立的文档识别接口也支持直接上传 PDF、Word、PPT
和常见的图片，提供纯文字直接提取和逐页保留排版的识别两种模式，每识别
1000 页只需要 1.5
元人民币。如果开发者把纯文本、代码或表格文件通过文件接口上传并内联拼进对话上下文中，也是完全免收工具解析费的。
DeepSeek
独立搜索接口将搜索与网页全文抓取解耦并以 5
元千次的价格大幅低于海外内置搜索与第三方检索工具
官方反复警告的合规下移，在账单和代码里是怎么落地的？
在了解工具能力和价格后，许多开发者还注意到一个细节。此次公告以醒目篇幅提醒，面向外部提供服务的开发者应启用高水位安全审核参数，并自行承担算法备案和内容审核的主体责任。不少人好奇，这究竟只是例行的法务免责声明，还是真的会反映在工程代码和接口账单上？
查阅
开放平台的服务条款
可以发现，关于平台只提供中立的接口、下游开发者需要自己进行大模型的登记备案和内容安全审核的规定，早在
2026 年 4 月 22
日就已经修订写入，并在几天后正式生效。为什么这次公告如此着重强调这一点？因为以前的接口只能支持纯文本对话，一旦放开了全网实时搜索、任意网页抓取和开箱即用的前端源码，任何人都可以在几分钟内构建一个带有实时联网能力的对话网站。平台希望出售这些组件，同时不替下游应用承担监管风险或补贴内容审核所需的算力。为此，官方在
模型的内容安全指南
中制定了一套职责与账单切分规则，将内容安全审核作为一个由开发者自费买单的收费项目。
第一笔开销是审核算力按模型输出单价收费。开发者按建议把安全审核开关调到高水位后，服务端审查输入和输出所消耗的算力会折算成安全词元，直接计入总输出词元账单，按
deepseek-flash
每百万输出词元 4
元人民币的单价收费。第二笔开销是触发违规拦截照样扣费。如果用户的提问未通过审核，接口直接返回
400
风险错误，但输入词元依然按缓存命中单价扣费；如果内置读链接工具抓回了目标网页，随后因未通过审核而返回禁止访问的错误块，这半毛钱的抓取费同样照收不误。
第三处工程细节落在流式输出的前端清屏要求上。流式输出时，文字是一个词一个词蹦出来的。如果生成中途触发了安全拦截，比如模型吐到一半的内容或用户上传的图片未通过审核，服务端无法撤回已经发出的文本块。这时服务端会停止生成并在末尾下发拒答信号，前面已生成的全部词元照常计费，同时官方要求客户端在收到拒答信号后必须自行清除界面上已展示的内容。翻看一下开源的
chat-demo
源码就能看到，前端接收流式回复的代码里专门写了拦截逻辑，一旦捕获到拒答状态，就立刻把界面上的思考过程和回答正文清空并替换成提示文案。
DeepSeek 应用全家桶 API
分为受限的内置对话模式与面向智能体开发者的独立工具接口两条路径
手头有项目的开发者，现在怎么接这套接口最划算？
看清了内置全家桶开关的绑定限制、独立工具接口的低价红利，以及安全审核的自费清屏机制后，手头有项目的开发者可以根据业务形态，按三条路径来做取舍。如果你正在开发自己的智能体或给工作流配工具，哪怕主力模型用的是
GPT 或
Claude，最划算的做法都是绕开对话接口里的内置全家桶开关。你可以申请一个
DeepSeek
密钥，只把独立搜索、网页抓取和文档识别这三个独立工具接口封装成普通的自定义工具函数。这样做既不会撞上封禁自定义工具的报错限制，又能凭借远低于市面同类服务的检索与识别单价，把原本昂贵的第三方工具账单降下九成以上。
如果你日常用 Claude Code 或 Codex
敲码，可以直接升级官方刚更新的接入配置。DeepSeek
已经在底层帮这两把刀躲过了内置开关的限制：Codex
的最新配置脚本默认用独立搜索和抓取接口，而 DeepSeek 的 Anthropic
兼容接口也在服务端做了专门适配，让 Claude Code
触发内置联网搜索时可以直接调通底层搜索引擎。
如果你只是想快速做个面向国内用户的纯聊天网页，而且不打算挂自己的业务工具，可以用
deepseek-flash
内置的全家桶开关加上
chat-demo
前端。但上线前要接受两个限制：模型采样参数固定、不能混用自定义工具；以及开启高水位安全审核、把安全词元计入成本，还要在前端收到拒答信号后自动清屏。
这套独立工具接口刚在 11 月 13
日上线，目前公开的技术文档和实测主要验证了它的接口形态和计费规则。它在长尾英文技术资料、反爬严密的垂直社区以及高并发峰值下的实际召回质量与稳定性，还有待大规模生产流量和第三方基准测试的检验。

items.text: innei published: 让 Agent 先问清楚、画出来、再证明：我的 Ryugi 工作流
items.title: 让 Agent 先问清楚、画出来、再证明：我的 Ryugi 工作流
items.content:
Ryugi (流儀)
—Ryugi is a set of interactive artifacts I built for coding agents. Whenever the agent needs to ask me questions or have me pick an approach, it puts them on interactive pages where I can answer directly: design decisions are written up as a document where I choose options item by item and leave sentence-level comments; UI proposals are laid out on a canvas for me to click and choose; and when the work is done, an acceptance page places approved designs side by side with live screenshots so I can approve or reject them group by group. Every choice I make on these pages feeds right back into the agent session that started it.
Repository
· Innei
523
ryugi
Ryugi (ryoo-ghee) — artifacts for coding agents: artboards of mockups, design docs, whiteboards, HTML benches and verify reports you comment on, with every comment sent back to the agent. Install artifacts only, or the full brainstorm → spec → TDD workflow. Claude Code, Codex and more.
JavaScript
The project here was the whiteboard inside my blog editor, haklex. Its editing features had always leaned on Excalidraw, which pulled in a heavy bundle and clashed with the rest of the editor's visual style. I wanted to drop the dependency and roll our own whiteboard around Excalidraw's data format, without touching a single field in existing articles.
From my opening sentence to `git push` took about half a day: two rounds of development, one release, and three downstream projects updated. I typed fewer than 20 messages in chat; wherever I had to make a call, it was turned into questions in a doc or mockups on a canvas. Here is how it went, step by step.
After one prompt: a doc that asks questions
My opening prompt was just one sentence: "Drop the excalidraw dependency and roll our own whiteboard based on its data structures."
The agent first inspected the code to confirm the scope of changes, then opened a design doc and put its questions directly into it, without following up in the chat box.
The questions were embedded right inside the document, each with a recommended option and the reasoning behind it; all I had to do was click my choice on the page. The first question was a fork in the road that determined how big v1 should be—everything that followed depended on it. For two of the questions I skipped the recommendation, and the next round simply picked up from what I chose.
After each round, the conclusions were merged into a "Decided" section, noting whether I made the decision or the agent made it for me. I could tell at a glance which items needed another look.
Section 4 of the design doc, "Decided": each conclusion is tagged with who decided it
After two rounds, the document was fleshed out into a full design spec. Before handing it back to me, the agent had an uninvolved reviewer agent do a cold read; it resolved most of the feedback on its own, leaving just two questions for me to settle.
自研白板编辑器：替换 @excalidraw/excalidraw · Ryugi
View “自研白板编辑器：替换 @excalidraw/excalidraw” on Ryugi Cloud, a document artifact.
Ryugi
"Should we discuss the UI?"
Once the document Q&A was done, I asked: "Should we discuss the UI?" The agent said yes—the design spec had marked the UI as "left to the implementer," but these are things you see every time you open the editor.
Text doesn't do UI justice, so it switched to a visual canvas: each group presented several options side by side, the recommended one highlighted with a red border, and sticky notes explaining the reasoning right beside them.
Round 1 decision fork on the UI canvas: three layout options side by side, with the recommended one outlined in red
Across two rounds and five groups, I went with the recommendations every time. With the options drawn out side by side, it was immediately clear which were good and which were bad. The selected mockups were linked into the design spec to guide both implementation and acceptance. Then I replied with "approve."
白板编辑器界面 · Ryugi
View “白板编辑器界面” on Ryugi Cloud, an artboard artifact.
Ryugi
Once approved, I didn't look at code again
Once approved, the agent broke the design spec into 19 small tasks and tackled them one by one on a separate branch.
Each task followed the same rhythm: write a failing test, watch it fail, write the implementation to make it pass, and commit. Whenever the agent made a call on its own—like minor details that diverged slightly from the spec—it logged it in a ledger. When the chat grew too long and was summarized, it kept working right from that ledger.
For over an hour, I didn't type a single word.
Review, then the acceptance page
Once all 19 tasks were finished, the agent handed the branch over to an independent reviewer agent that had played no part in development. For every issue flagged, it reproduced it with a failing test before writing the fix.
Then it spun up the editor in a real browser, took screenshots and screen recordings, and put together an acceptance page: my approved canvas designs on the left, and how it actually looked running on the right.
Acceptance page: approved design, live screenshot, and screen recording side by side
All I had to do was review each group and approve or reject it. I left a comment on one mockup; it made the fix, took a new screenshot, and placed it right back in the same spot for me to review. Anything it couldn't verify was listed separately on the page, instead of being mixed in with "Completed."
白板编辑器界面 · Ryugi
View “白板编辑器界面” on Ryugi Cloud, an artboard artifact.
Ryugi
Round two: starting from a reference image
Next, I wanted the whiteboard to look sharper. I pasted a reference image featuring clean headings, drop-shadowed sticky notes, and illustrative stickers, and asked whether stock Excalidraw could pull off that aesthetic.
It broke down the elements in the image one by one—what we could already draw, what capabilities were missing—and even guessed I might want an AI to do the drawing. I replied with one sentence: only build general-purpose drawing capabilities.
Next was the same process: open a new design doc, then three rounds of Q&A. In round three, putting rich-text cards on the whiteboard was my own idea. After a cold read, the reviewer agent flagged two questions that needed my call; the agent added its recommendations, I replied with two numbers, approved, and let it implement and review.
The acceptance page for this round measured directly against my reference image: the reference on the left, the recreation inside our editor on the right.
Round 2 acceptance: reference image side by side with the in-editor recreation
白板绘制能力扩展：阴影、SVG 元素、富文本卡片 · Ryugi
View “白板绘制能力扩展：阴影、SVG 元素、富文本卡片” on Ryugi Cloud, a document artifact.
Ryugi
Verify · 白板绘制能力扩展 · Ryugi
View “Verify · 白板绘制能力扩展” on Ryugi Cloud, an artboard artifact.
Ryugi
Release, then downstream projects
With both rounds approved, I asked: "Can we release now, and then adapt the downstream projects?" It cut a new release, then went through three projects using the editor one by one—bumping the dependency, running tests, and verifying in a browser that the whiteboard rendered properly.
Downstream results were posted right on the acceptance page as well, with one screenshot for light mode and one for dark.
The same whiteboard in downstream projects: light and dark mode
Throughout the entire process, logging in to authenticate the npm release was the only thing that needed my manual login—that was the one step the agent couldn't do for me.
What I actually said in the chat
Looking back, nearly everything I typed in chat over that half-day is captured right here:
Time
What I said
What happened next
12:26
Drop the excalidraw dependency and roll our own whiteboard based on its data structures
Read code, opened design doc
13:04
Should we discuss the UI?
Opened canvas for UI discussion
13:18
approve
Sliced tasks, started implementation
16:35
This looks about ready. Now let's work on extra features.
Compared against reference image, kicked off Round 2
16:38
Let's only build general-purpose drawing capabilities
Narrowed scope, opened new doc
17:04
approve
Implemented Round 2
17:56
Can we release now, and then adapt the downstream projects?
Published release, adapted downstream projects
20:06
push
Pushed to remote
Every other decision was made by clicking options in docs, picking mockups on a canvas, or signing off on the acceptance page. I didn't have to scroll through chat history to find what the agent said; every decision stayed on the page, and all the implementation and acceptance were checked against those same pages.
Boundaries
This workflow doesn't make judgment calls for me. If I skip an open-ended question, it fills in its best guess and flags it, leaving me to decide whether to review it. The acceptance page lists what it couldn't verify, and deciding whether to test further is up to me. What it does is put decisions right in front of me, so I can see at a glance what is settled and what isn't.
Ryugi is open source (
github.com/Innei/ryugi
). In your terminal, run
npx ryugi-artifacts install
, and select the agent you use to install it. The two design docs, canvas, and acceptance pages mentioned here are all public, so you can see them in their original form.

items.title: Migrating from React Native to UIKit in 87 Hours: Hollow Out the Data Layer, Then Invert the Host
items.content:
Lody iOS started out on Expo + React Native. By October, the chat timeline, composer, Live Activity, and Share Extension had all been rewritten in UIKit—roughly 61,000 lines of Swift alongside 37,000 lines of TypeScript. What remained of React Native was mostly routing and screen-level glue: navigation was split half in Expo Router and half in native code, and every build still ran through
expo prebuild
, Metro, and CocoaPods.
Repository
· innei-dev
531
lody-ios
Independent iOS client for Lody — native chat, sessions, and coding-agent collaboration on iPhone
Swift
On the night of October 24, I decided to remove React Native entirely and replace the remaining screens with UIKit one by one. On the morning of October 28,
#96
merged into
main
, deleting the RN runtime after roughly three and a half days (87 hours) across 482 files (+25,700 / −37,500 lines). I then spent the next three days reorganizing the directory structure around explicit dependency layers.
Whiteboard
Finishing the cutover in 87 hours was only possible because the real strangler-fig work had started six weeks earlier. Between early September and mid-October, diff rendering, the chat timeline, and the rich-text composer were extracted into standalone packages, followed by
cloud-runtime
on October 11. By the time the migration started on October 24, the app was already layered like this:
Whiteboard
In other words, React Native had already been hollowed out into a thin outer shell: the heavy UI primitives were standalone packages, and the data runtime had lived inside a Swift-owned offscreen
WKWebView
from day one. The migration came down to three questions:
Where should the cross-platform boundary live once coding agents make native UI cheap? How do you invert the host of a 100k-line app without freezing trunk? And when offline verification holds pixel diffs to 0.00026, which four regressions still slip through the cracks?
1. The Shifting Premise: Moving the Shared Boundary from UI to Data
We originally chose React Native with a future Android client in mind. The bet was to keep both the data layer and the UI abstraction in RN: React components would describe screen layouts, while iOS and Android would merely supply the underlying native views. When it came time to build Android, we would only need view implementations—neither the data layer nor screen structures would have to be rewritten.
Whiteboard
The left side shows that original bet; the right side shows where we landed. The shared cross-platform boundary moved down from UI to a headless data layer:
cloud-runtime
runs inside an offscreen WebView, iOS and a future Android client implement the same versioned contract, and each platform writes its UI natively.
Two shifts broke the original equilibrium. First,
coding agents collapsed the marginal cost of native UI
. Writing a separate UI per platform used to be the exact expense RN was meant to save. In this migration, the remaining screens were rewritten in batches alongside coding agents in three and a half days. Once the one-time cost of writing native screens drops that low, paying an ongoing abstraction tax to avoid it no longer pencils out.
Second,
the three-layer translation tax in navigation
. Navigation bars, toolbars, and sheets ultimately end up as UIKit, but in RN they had to pass through three layers of translation to get there:
Whiteboard
On the left, every layer maintains its own state and assumptions. As soon as iOS 26 glass styling, iPad split views, and iPhone Duo foldable layouts entered the picture, bugs clustered in the seams between layers (the gray annotations show a few issues hit while adapting for Duo). Our patch against
react-native-screens
started on September 10 and was revised 11 times before deletion. On the right, there is no middleman—each view controller owns its navigation items directly.
Each individual glitch was patchable, but every fix added another layer of state translation between RN and UIKit. On October 17, I got wide-screen layouts working for iPad and iPhone Duo in RN, and the result still felt rough. A week later, I decided to stop patching and go all-in on native.
2. The Strangler-Fig Inversion: Hollow Out First, Flip the Host Second
To swap out the host without halting feature work on
main
, we couldn't start by rewriting screens. We had to unwind a reverse dependency chain: six weeks of preparatory extraction to hollow out the shell, followed by three sequential locks once the cutover began.
Six Weeks of Prep: Stripping Out Heavy Views and Data Until Only Routing and Context Remained
The timeline below lays out the extractions between September 6 and October 24 across two tracks—the data layer and UI primitives:
The three heaviest UI subsystems went first: diff rendering (
dom-webview
), the chat timeline (ChatKit), and the rich-text composer (
lexical-swift
). They were already written in Swift or self-contained DOM bundles that RN screens simply mounted. When we later replaced screens one by one, the new UIKit view controllers imported those packages directly without having to untangle view logic mid-flight.
Repository
· Innei
3
ChatKit
UIKit chat primitives: streaming text reveal, attachment strip, glass surface. iOS 26, Swift 6.
Swift
The data layer was never inside RN to begin with. Swift owned an offscreen
WKWebView
where sync, local replicas, and retries ran; RN only ever received read-only projections for display. On October 11, that runtime and its protocol types were extracted into
@lody/cloud-runtime
.
Earlier, on September 8, the cloud code had already been split by domain into
auth
,
catalog
, and
send
—the exact three boundaries that would become Swift's
AuthSession
,
CatalogSession
, and
Outbox
on October 25. By the night of October 24, all RN held besides routing was the state inside five root Context providers.
Lock 1: Establish a Versioned Contract and Sink State into Swift
Why didn't day one touch a single screen? Because replacing screens incrementally required UIKit to own navigation first, turning each remaining RN screen into an independently hosted root view. Once screens become separate root views, React Context on a single root component can no longer span across them—so global state had to leave RN first. And for Swift services and native screens to talk to the offscreen runtime without going through RN, Swift and the runtime needed a formal contract.
Previously, Swift invoked the runtime by concatenating raw JS strings, which was tolerable when the RN host was the only caller. Now native screens needed to call the runtime directly—and a future Android host would need the exact same surface—so the very first commit on October 24 replaced string interpolation with a schema-driven contract:
The Zod schema in
cloud-runtime
became the single source of truth. Types for every platform are generated from it, and the host and runtime only exchange envelopes carrying a schema version (
v
) and instance generation (
gen
). Version mismatches fail the handshake immediately, and messages from stale WebView generations are dropped on sight. Swapping the host—or adding a new platform—never touches the runtime.
Over the next 23 hours, the five React Contexts on the RN root were consolidated into four single-owner Swift services. The left side shows the old RN root provider tree; the right side shows how both RN and UIKit screens read state afterward:
Each slice of state has a single owner in Swift. Remaining RN screens and new UIKit screens read the same synchronous JSON snapshot and subscribe to the same change event. Splitting screens into separate root views no longer affected shared state—and as a security bonus, long-lived Better Auth credentials now stayed strictly in Swift and Keychain without ever entering the JS context. By the evening of October 25, once
Outbox
landed in Swift and
CatalogProvider
was deleted, the root Context tree was empty.
Lock 2: Invert the Host so UIKit Wraps RN Screens
With state out of the way, Expo Router still owned navigation. As long as RN owned navigation, native views could only live as child components inside RN screens—we could never replace a whole screen. The pivotal move was inverting the host relationship: UIKit took over the window and navigation chrome, demoting the remaining RN screens into leaf views hosted inside UIKit containers. The diagram below shows the three stages of the host; this step moved us from left to center:
Whiteboard
In that middle transitional state, each unmigrated RN screen became an isolated surface backed by a single shared
RCTHost
. The outer UIKit container didn't care whether a destination was rendered by an RN surface or a native view controller, unlocking true screen-by-screen replacement without blast radius across pages. (Earlier on iPad, I had tried reparenting a mounted RN view into a different superview, which silently broke touch press handling; giving each screen its own surface avoided that trap entirely.)
The new UIKit shell went in behind a launch flag first. Compact iPhone navigation and regular-width iPad split navigation were wired up in turn; once both ran cleanly, Expo Router was deleted in the early hours of October 26—six hours from feature flag to router removal.
Lock 3: Cut the Umbilical Cord—Remove the RN Runtime and Build Chain
Once all remaining RN leaf screens were replaced with UIKit (covered in the next section), the app still booted through Expo's
AppDelegate
and every build still ran through
expo prebuild
and Metro.
#96
severed that final layer—moving from the center of the host diagram to the far right: a native
AppDelegate
/
SceneDelegate
boots
LodyApplication
directly, giving lifecycle, deep links, push notifications, and the share inbox native owners. The build pipeline flipped with it:
The
ios/
directory is no longer wiped and regenerated by
prebuild
; the Xcode project is generated deterministically from a committed
project.yml
via XcodeGen. React, Expo, Hermes, and the stack of
react-native-screens
patches were deleted together. Only the headless WebView runtime bundle continues to be built with
pnpm
—the one layer that never changed from start to finish.

· innei-dev/lody-ios

3. Deterministic Verification and Its Cracks: 0.00026 Pixel Diffs vs. 4 Escaped Regressions
Between October 26 and October 28, rewriting every remaining screen in UIKit within 48 hours—without breaking
main
—would have been impossible with manual QA. What made the blitz safe was an offline verification harness; what makes it interesting in hindsight are the four bugs that still escaped it.
Leaf-to-Trunk Replacement: Isolating Every Screen Behind a Single Service Seam
Once the UIKit shell was in charge, every native screen was built around the exact same decoupled structure:
A view controller's only I/O is a
service
closure. Production routes inject the
live
implementation (wired to
DataRuntime
,
Catalog
, and
Outbox
); Debug scenes inject a
scripted
implementation returning fixed fixtures. Both paths run the exact same view controller. Before flipping any screen, we registered an offline Debug scene and a
verify:ui
behavioral test that deep-linked straight into it—no login, no cloud, and no local agent daemon required—running the identical assertion suite before and after the swap.
With offline assertions in place, replacement proceeded mechanically from leaves to trunk. On October 26, all Settings sub-screens, Home, and Project screens moved first; that night, the complex Session screen was built in UIKit behind a Debug fixture. On October 27, the remaining screens were conquered in a stack of eight PRs (
#87
–
#94
): message editing, message details, tool details, permissions, PR view, and file browser, followed by flipping the production Session entry point to native and finishing Home and iPad navigation. On the morning of October 28,
#86
and the entire PR stack merged together.

When
#96
deleted the RN runtime hours later, the offline UI suite ran directly against the pure native build. Across 20 screenshots of the new-session form compared pixel-by-pixel against the previous build, the maximum diff was
0.00026
.
Where the Harness Cracked: How 4 Regressions Escaped a 0.00026 Pixel Gate
Even with screenshot diffs pinned to the fourth decimal place and core flows working cleanly, four regressions still surfaced after cutover. Looking at them side by side is revealing—every single one lived on the seam between offline scripted scenes and the real runtime environment:
Whiteboard
The test entry point had no test of its own
: The Debug screen dispatches every offline scene, yet had no test case covering itself. After converting to UIKit, it regressed into an ungrouped flat list missing its navigation bar.
Build configuration skew (Debug vs. Release)
: Debug scenes were only registered under
Debug
and
UI Verify
build configurations, and automated checks never ran against
Release
. Long-pressing the Settings button in TestFlight builds triggered an unregistered route and crashed immediately.
Offline stubs bypassed the OS modal hierarchy
: During Device Flow sign-in,
SFSafariViewController
presents over the welcome screen; after authorization completed, dismissing closed only Safari while leaving the welcome screen stuck underneath. Because the "open browser" step in the offline fixture was a no-op stub, the real system modal stack was never exercised.
Static fixtures skipped async teardown races in the live runtime
: Opening a session from a push notification caused the previous screen's delayed
deinit
to close the session the new screen had just opened. Offline scenes fed synchronous scripted data without a live
DataRuntime
, so that cross-controller lifecycle race never fired under test.
4. Post-Merge Convergence: Freeze Paths During Cutover, Layer by Dependency After
Throughout the 87-hour sprint, I followed one strict rule:
never move files while changing behavior
. Keeping file paths frozen meant every commit was a pure implementation swap—easy to review and trivial to
git bisect
if something broke. The trade-off was that when
#96
landed, all 557 Swift files were still sitting inside the legacy Expo module directory, mixing view controllers, data sessions, and platform glue. Only after behavior was locked down did I put on the refactoring hat for three days of structural layering, again doing one thing per step:
Step 1: Move files without splitting code.
With RN gone,
apps/mobile
and the Expo module path were vestigial. All Swift sources were moved wholesale into a single Swift package,
LodyKit
, while dependencies switched from CocoaPods to SPM.
Step 2: Split along the
import UIKit
boundary.
Auth, catalog, outbox, the data runtime host, session models, and copy were extracted into
LodyData
—a module that never imports UIKit and compiles and tests in isolation. Whenever the data layer needs a platform side effect (opening URLs, requesting background execution time, showing a toast, presenting an auth browser, or writing a Share Extension snapshot), it calls the
LodyHost
protocol, which the top-level App target implements and injects.
Step 3: Flatten the project hierarchy.
The repository root became the Xcode project root, eliminating the
apps/
wrapper. Finally, the remaining UI code in
LodyKit
was folded back into the App target—the App was its only consumer, while views shared with the Share Extension moved into
Shared/UIKit
as direct source references. Keeping a separate UI package only added ceremony around access control, so the App target is now organized directly into
Application
,
Navigation
,
ViewControllers
,
Views
,
Services
, and
Platform
.
The resulting dependency graph flows strictly in one direction—the lower a layer sits, the less it knows about UI:
Whiteboard
The repository root is the Xcode project root, generated from the committed
project.yml
; the generated
Lody.xcodeproj
is never edited by hand.
Takeaways for Anyone Planning a Similar Migration
Looking back, the critical factor wasn't how fast UIKit views could be written—it was respecting a strict sequence of dependency locks where each step unlocked the physical precondition for the next:
Start by deciding
which layer actually deserves to be shared
. React Native's cross-platform leverage lives in UI; once coding agents make platform-native UI cheap to write, it pays to push the shared boundary down into a headless data runtime behind a versioned contract. Extract heavy UI primitives first, sink shared state out of RN, and then invert the navigation host—once a native shell can host legacy RN screens as isolated leaves, every remaining screen can be replaced and verified independently. And when designing your verification harness, remember to test the test entry point itself,
Release
build flags, real OS modal stacks, and async teardown across live runtime sessions.
I'm not a veteran iOS engineer, and this layering reflects how I reasoned through the problem rather than established orthodoxy. I'm still weighing trade-offs—like whether running a JS data runtime inside an offscreen WebView is worth it long-term, whether protocol injection via
LodyHost
is the cleanest way to handle platform side effects, or whether keeping App UI code in folders rather than SPM packages will hold up as the codebase grows. If you've been through a similar migration or would structure this differently, I'd love to hear your thoughts in the comments.

items.title: 十个月，给 LobeHub 换掉 Ant Design：向 Base UI 与 StyleX 的渐进式迁移
items.content:
The starting point: a performance tuning pass
During my first month at LobeHub, I ran a performance optimization pass, documented with benchmarks in
"Performance and DX Optimizations at LobeHub"
. The heaviest bottlenecks in that pass were all style-related: CSS-in-JS Flexbox components like react-layout-kit numbered in the hundreds on a single page, each generating CSS; the
useStyle
running across almost every component recalculated styles on every re-render; and a single antd Tooltip took 0.5ms on its own. The first two could be fixed by switching styling solutions, but Tooltip required a full rewrite. I rebuilt both it and Popover with Base UI—the first time Base UI was used in lobe-ui.
With those fixes in place, the remaining overhead came from antd components themselves. Since antd's UI was also notoriously hard to customize deeply, replacing it was the obvious next move. I had wanted to do this for a while, but never started because manually rewriting a codebase of this size was unrealistic, and AI wasn't capable enough yet.
When we actually started, this was what we were facing:
@lobehub/ui
had almost a hundred component modules, with behavior tightly coupled to antd and all component styles written in Emotion-based
antd-style
, which generated CSS at runtime and injected it into the document on every page load. Downstream, five ecosystem libraries—icons, editor, charts, tts, and fluent-emoji—declared it as a peer dependency, and at the top layer, hundreds of business files in lobe-chat directly imported from
import ... from 'antd'
. Meanwhile, product features shipped weekly, so maintaining a long-running rewrite branch wasn't an option. The entire migration had to happen without interrupting delivery, split into two parallel tracks: first swap out the underlying component foundation from antd to Base UI, then switch styling from runtime Emotion to compile-time StyleX.
Letting old and new components coexist in the same package
lobe-ui#448
rewrote Tooltip. Beyond performance gains, it also resolved seven Linear issues: positioning drift, tooltips failing to dismiss, and elements snapping back to (0, 0) when their host unmounted. Base UI is headless, providing only behavior and accessibility while leaving DOM structure and styling to us, so we could customize everything freely without fighting antd's limitations.
The next question was how to make the transition. With weekly product releases and several downstream libraries tracking our changes, ripping out antd all at once wasn't practical. Instead, I opted for coexistence: build new components with Base UI, package them alongside the antd versions, and migrate product call sites one component at a time. Throughout January 2026, we gradually added
lobe-ui#444
's Base UI Menu–based DropdownMenu and ContextMenu, alongside LobeSwitch and LobeSelect. To avoid name clashes with their antd counterparts, they initially carried a Lobe prefix or a V2 suffix.
On March 2,
lobe-ui#467
released v5, formalizing this coexistence in the package structure: adding a
@lobehub/ui/base-ui
subpath where LobeSelect and LobeSwitch were moved (dropping their prefixes), while DropdownMenu, Toast, ContextMenu, and ScrollArea were exported from there as well. The package itself also became ESM-only. Subsequent components followed the exact same pattern: the implementation lived under
src/base-ui/
, while the root entry only re-exported it. For instance, when
lobe-ui#486
migrated Popover,
@lobehub/ui
and
@lobehub/ui/base-ui
were both valid, requiring zero changes in product code. From here on, migrating a component took just two steps: write the new implementation under base-ui, then switch the call sites in product code.
Components had to be drop-in replacements, locked down with linting once migrated
Between March and September, components were ported into base-ui roughly in this order: overlays, basic controls, forms, display, and layout.
Overlays first
This came down to two reasons. To begin with, overlays naturally belong together: Dropdown, Popover, Tooltip, Modal, and Drawer all share floating positioning and stacking management, making them ideal to tackle together. Later,
lobe-ui#518
unified their z-index management under a single layer manager. The second reason was how Modal was structured. Antd's Modal is primarily declarative, requiring components to be mounted on the React tree in advance:
open
is
false
, its children still render, re-rendering whenever ancestor state updates. With multiple Modals on a page, that overhead adds up on every single render. An imperative Modal creates an instance only when invoked and destroys it when closed, shifting the cost to the user action that opens it. I previously wrote about this in
"Why I Recommend Imperative Modals,"
and base-ui's Modal has supported both imperative and declarative patterns since its
first release
.
In the top example, every closed Modal participates in every render; in the bottom example, only the active Modal exists in the tree.
Migration windows by component category
After overlays came basic controls, forms, and display components. They all followed the exact same workflow: merge the new component into base-ui, switch product call sites over, and finally ban the legacy import via ESLint. Each bar below runs from when the new component merged to when the legacy import was banned:
A stark dividing line is visible around August. Before August, taking a component category from initial merge to banning legacy imports took weeks or months: Modal and Select took nearly four months, and form controls took 36 days. After August, Drawer took 5 days, Alert 6 days, Skeleton 3 days, DraggablePanel and Tree 2 days each, while ActionIcon, Avatar, Tag, and Text took just 1 day combined. The migration process hadn't changed—what changed was the models. Anthropic released Claude Fable 5 on June 9 and Claude Opus 5 on July 24. To me, Opus 5 felt exceptionally strong at front-end tasks, and at half the price of Fable 5, it cost about the same as Opus 4.8. By August, commits in lobe-chat switched from Opus 4.8 to Opus 5, and Fable 5 usage was rising too. The bars for Tabs and Segmented are also very short, but only because the initial preset banned five components all at once on June 26—not because they migrated faster.
Components like DropdownMenu, Tooltip, and Popover were replaced in place at the root entry point without legacy versions to ban, so they aren't shown in the chart. Commits for each component:
Modal
,
Menu
,
Tooltip
,
Button
,
Form controls
,
Drawer
,
Alert
,
ActionIcon and three others
,
Skeleton
,
DraggablePanel
, and
Tree
.
Each new component had to be a drop-in replacement, matching the old version in both API and visuals so switching only meant changing import paths. In lobe-ui#621, Tag's color resolution was ported straight from the old implementation: 13 preset colors, 5 system colors, and and all four variants (solid, filled, outlined, borderless) across three sizes had to match. Avatar replaced antd Avatar with native
img
, keeping the fallback on load failure and the +N counter for AvatarGroup. After Drawer merged, a separate
commit
followed to align its surface, edges, and drop shadows with antd Drawer.
The ban rules lived in lobe-ui's built-in ESLint preset, inherited directly by product projects. The
initial preset
on June 26 deprecated and banned imports of five antd-based wrappers: Button, Modal, Segmented, Select, and Tabs. When that first version went live, product code still had numerous legacy calls, which were temporarily grandfathered via an allowlist (detailed in the next section). From that point on, rules for each component category were added to the preset only after downstream projects had cleared all legacy imports. The PR description in
lobe-ui#610
was blunt: downstream migrations had removed legacy imports for these components, and this PR turned the migration boundary into an enforceable lint rule. That way, new code couldn't introduce old patterns, and legacy usage could only ever go down.
On the product side: freeze new usage, then clear legacy code category by category
Each time lobe-ui finished migrating a component category, lobe-chat had to update corresponding call sites. The chart below shows the number of files directly importing antd in lobe-chat, sampled biweekly:
Until mid-June, this line kept rising—climbing from 338 in mid-February to 485 on June 15. While legacy calls were being replaced, new features continued using antd. By then, the team had already delegated most product coding to AI, and component precedence had long been codified into
AGENTS.md
and react skills:
@lobehub/ui/base-ui
Any component available in it had to be imported from it, with same-named components at the root entry point off-limits, leaving antd strictly as a fallback when neither had it. Agents routinely ignored this. Because training data and hundreds of existing files demonstrated antd patterns, PRs for new features kept using legacy components even after lobe-ui published replacements. To an agent, docs are merely suggestions. The only way to stop them was to make violations break the build: ESLint fails directly, and lint-staged runs the same checks in pre-commit hooks to block the commit.
That was precisely what
lobehub#16334
did on June 26: it adopted lobe-ui's ESLint preset, banning the five legacy wrappers (Button, Modal, Segmented, Select, Tabs) as well as antd-style's
createStyles
; existing call sites (354 in total) were added to
eslint-suppressions.json
for temporary exemption, while any new violations failed immediately. Afterward, whenever a batch was migrated, we ran
eslint --prune-suppressions
, ensuring the allowlist only ever shrank.
Legacy code was cleared category by category: each PR targeted only one component category, but covered the entire repository. The count dropped slowly over the summer, followed by a steep drop in early October.
lobehub#20247
touched 285 files in one go, swapping out all remaining instances of Table, DatePicker, Menu, List, Input variants, and more, eliminating 163 files with direct antd imports. The PR included before-and-after screenshots compared against canary for verification, and five component library issues caught along the way were patched in
lobe-ui#675
. Next,
lobehub#20317
migrated forms, removing another 63 files;
lobehub#20408
updated menu item types to lobe-ui's, shedding 21 files; finally,
lobehub#20503
cleaned up the remainder. The two files still remaining on November 1 in the chart are test fixtures for alint.
Behavioral discrepancies are harder to catch than visual differences
Visual differences are easy to spot by comparing screenshots side by side, but behavioral discrepancies usually don't surface until a user saves data. After lobehub#20317 migrated forms to base-ui, the values returned on submit differed between the two:
antd Form
base-ui Form
Returned on submit

Form.Item
fields only
Entire form store

initialValues
extra keys
